The densities of 3d series elements are generally lower than those of the corresponding s-block elements.

questions.solution:

However, the nuclear charge of 5d elements is higher by 32 units. Because the 4f electrons provide poor shielding, the effective nuclear charge acting on the outer valence electrons in 5d elements is significantly greater. As a result, the first ionization enthalpies of 5d elements are generally higher than those of the corresponding 3d and 4d elements.

Option 2 is true but is due to the maximum number of unpaired d-electrons contributing to strong metallic bonding.

Answer: The first ionization enthalpies of 5d series elements are generally higher than those of the corresponding 3d and 4d series elements.

questions.question: A transition metal $\text{M}$ belongs to the $3d$ series and possesses the highest melting point among the elements of this series. What is the spin-only magnetic moment of the $\text{M}^{3+}$ ion?
questions.solution:
In the $3d$ transition series, the melting point generally increases with the number of unpaired electrons, reaching a maximum at chromium ($\text{Cr}$), which has a $3d^{5} 4s^{1}$ configuration. (Manganese shows an anomalous dip and does not have the highest melting point).

Thus, the metal $\text{M}$ is Chromium ($\text{Cr}$).

The electronic configuration of $\text{Cr}$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{5} 4s^{1}$.

The electronic configuration of the $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{3}$.

Number of unpaired electrons ($n$) = $3$.

The spin-only magnetic moment ($\mu$) is given by $\sqrt{n(n+2)} \text{ BM}$.

$\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87 \text{ BM}$.

Choosing $\text{Mn}$ incorrectly as the metal with the highest melting point would lead to $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ ($3d^{4}$), giving $4.90 \text{ BM}$. Calculating the magnetic moment for the neutral $\text{Cr}$ atom ($n=6$) would incorrectly give $6.93 \text{ BM}$.

Answer: $3.87 \text{ BM}$

questions.solution:
In an acidic medium, $KMnO_4$ oxidises iodide ($I^-$) to iodine ($I_2$) and itself gets reduced to $Mn^{2+}$.
The n-factor for $KI$ is $1$ (since $2I^- \rightarrow I_2 + 2e^-$, so $1$ mole of $I^-$ loses $1$ mole of $e^-$).
The n-factor for $KMnO_4$ is $5$ ($Mn^{+7} \rightarrow Mn^{+2}$).
Equating the number of equivalents:
Moles of $KMnO_4 \times 5 = \text{Moles of } KI \times 1$
$n_1 \times 5 = 1 \times 1 \Rightarrow n_1 = \dfrac{1}{5}$ moles.

In a faintly alkaline medium, $KMnO_4$ oxidises iodide ($I^-$) to iodate ($IO_3^-$) and itself gets reduced to $MnO_2$.
The n-factor for $KI$ is $6$ ($I^- \rightarrow IO_3^-$, change in oxidation state from $-1$ to $+5$).
The n-factor for $KMnO_4$ is $3$ ($Mn^{+7} \rightarrow Mn^{+4}$).
Equating the number of equivalents:
Moles of $KMnO_4 \times 3 = \text{Moles of } KI \times 6$
$n_2 \times 3 = 1 \times 6 \Rightarrow n_2 = 2$ moles.

The required ratio is $n_1 : n_2 = \dfrac{1}{5} : 2 = 1 : 10$.

Answer: $1:10$
